name: Instant Trade Quote
tagline: Quoting tool for tradespeople: build a priced quote from a job description and send it as a branded PDF.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanics of a quoting tool are unglamorous and very buildable: a price book, line items with quantities, labour hours, markup, tax, a template, a PDF, an email. An agent will get you there in a weekend and the output can look better than most quotes a customer receives. What it cannot hand you is the priced catalogue, the tax logic you actually need for your region, or the accept-and-sign flow that turns a quote into a signed job. It also will not follow you up a ladder, which is where quotes get written. So: yes for the document, no for the field workflow, and you will be typing your own rates in for a while.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you pick line items from your own price book, set quantities and markup, and export or email a branded PDF quote with a running total and quote history.
requirements: Node 20+ and a machine or small VPS to run it on
Your own price list: materials, labour rates, markup rules
SMTP credentials in .env if you want to email quotes
A domain with SPF and DKIM set up, or quotes land in spam
Your logo and payment terms text
whatYouLose: A maintained materials and labour price book you did not have to type in
A phone-friendly, offline-tolerant way to quote while standing in someone's kitchen
Client-facing accept, e-sign and deposit payment, so quotes convert without a phone call
Accounting handoff: pushing accepted quotes into Xero, QuickBooks or invoicing without retyping
Email deliverability and tracking that someone else babysits
moatNotes: The defensible part of quoting software is the catalogue and the regional tax and margin rules, not the PDF.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a trade business is not short of software, it is short of evenings. Paying a few tens of dollars a month to have rates already loaded, quotes accepted online, and accepted quotes turn into invoices is a cheap trade against an hour of your own admin time. The DIY version wins on control and costs nothing to run, but it only pays off if you enjoy maintaining a price book and are happy quoting from a laptop rather than a phone in a van.
notes: The PDF is the easy half. The half that eats your weekend is entering every material price you use and keeping it current.
prompt:
Build a local-first quoting app for a single trade business. No accounts, no cloud services, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Tailwind for styling, nodemailer for email. Everything runs with `npm run dev` on localhost. No auth, it is single user on one machine.

Data model in SQLite:
- settings: business name, ABN/tax id, logo path, default tax rate, default markup percent, payment terms text, quote number prefix
- price_items: code, description, unit (each, m, m2, hour), cost, default_markup, category
- clients: name, email, phone, site address
- quotes: number, client_id, status (draft, sent, accepted, declined), issued_at, valid_until, notes, totals snapshot
- quote_lines: quote_id, price_item_id nullable, description, qty, unit, unit_cost, markup_percent, line_total

Screens:
1. Price book CRUD with CSV import and export so the user can bulk load their own rates.
2. Quote builder: pick a client, add lines by searching the price book or typing a free line, edit qty and markup inline, live subtotal, tax, total, and a margin readout in dollars and percent.
3. Quote list filtered by status with a duplicate-quote action.
4. Public-looking quote view at /quotes/[number]/print styled for A4 print with logo, line items, totals, terms, and a clean print stylesheet. PDF is produced by the browser print dialog, do not add a PDF library.

Email: one button that sends the quote as an HTML email with a link to the print view, using SMTP_HOST, SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASS, SMTP_FROM from .env. If SMTP vars are missing, disable the button and say so plainly.

In scope: quote math including per-line markup and a single tax rate, quote numbering, status changes, CSV price book import, print view.
Out of scope, do not build: e-signature, online payments, multi-user, accounting integrations, mobile app, offline sync, supplier price feeds.

Seed the database with about 20 fake price items across materials and labour so the app is usable on first run. Include a README with setup, .env.example, and one paragraph explaining that the price book is the user's job to fill in.
